Chapter 3 · Origins · c. 500 a. C.–200 d. C.

Philosophy and medicine in Antiquity

Alcmaeon, Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics and Galen: the brain, the humours, memory and emotions as objects of reasoning.

The word "psychology" comes from the Greek psyche, which meant breath, life and, gradually, soul or mind. In ancient Greece, philosophers and physicians began to look for natural explanations of what had once been attributed to the gods.

What were people trying to understand?

Where thought resides, how we perceive and remember, what emotions are and why people have different characters. Also what mental illness is: a divine punishment or an imbalance of the body.

With what methods?

Philosophical reasoning, clinical observation and, in some cases, the dissection of animals. The Hippocratic text On the Sacred Disease (around 400 BCE) argues that epilepsy is no more sacred than any other illness and that it originates in the brain. It is a statement of principle: look for natural causes.

Who took part?

Alcmaeon of Croton (fifth century BCE) proposed that the brain, not the heart, is the organ of thought and sensation. Hippocratic medicine explained health as a balance of four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile); "melancholy" literally means black bile. Plato divided the soul into three parts, reason, spirit and appetite, and compared their relationship to a charioteer driving two horses. Aristotle, in On the Soul and his short treatises on memory and dreams, described how we recall one thing from another through similarity, contrast or contiguity, an idea that would return in associationism two thousand years later. The Stoics, such as Epictetus, held that we are disturbed not by things but by our opinions about them. In Rome, Galen (second century) showed through animal experiments that the nerves arise from the brain and spinal cord, and turned the humours into a theory of temperaments: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic.

What did it contribute?

  • The search for natural causes of behaviour and mental suffering.
  • The brain as the seat of the mind, although the idea took a long time to prevail.
  • The laws of association, the basis of many theories of learning and memory.
  • A link between thought and emotion that explicitly inspired the cognitive therapies of the twentieth century.

What was revised later?

Humoral theory dominated European and Islamic medicine for more than a thousand years, until anatomy, physiology and chemistry dismantled it between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. What survived of the four temperaments is the intuition that people differ in stable ways, which personality psychology now studies with other methods. Aristotle, for his part, believed that the heart was the centre of sensation and that the brain served to cool the blood: great minds get things wrong too.

"Men are disturbed not by things, but by the opinions about things" (Epictetus). Albert Ellis quoted this line when explaining his therapy.
